items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Temperature Control in Greenhouses: A DQN-Based Framework and Experimental Evaluation
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence into controlled environment agriculture represents a transformative opportunity for addressing global food security challenges while promoting sustainable resource utilisation. This paper presents a comprehensive Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for optimizing greenhouse temperature management, leveraging data from the second edition of the Autonomous Greenhouse Challenge. We formulate the climate control problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and implement a Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent that learns to regulate temperature through discrete actions: heating, cooling, or maintaining the current state. Our methodology incorporates a sophisticated reward function that balances multiple objectives, including maintaining optimal growing conditions, minimizing energy consumption, and ensuring temperature stability. The agent is trained and evaluated on a subset of the 2019 challenge dataset, specifically utilizing measurements from the Reference team's compartment to ensure data consistency and reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that the RL agent effectively learns an adaptive control policy, achieving an average comfort zone occupancy of 40.1\% across diverse starting conditions while demonstrating appropriate action selection based on environmental state. The agent exhibits particularly strong performance when initialised within the optimal temperature range, achieving 100\% comfort zone occupancy in multiple evaluation episodes. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI-driven agricultural automation by providing a reproducible methodology, comprehensive performance analysis, and insights into the practical challenges of implementing RL systems in real-world greenhouse environments. The findings suggest that RL approaches offer a viable path toward autonomous greenhouse management with potential benefits for crop yield optimization and energy efficiency.

items.title: Designing a Human–AI Collaborative Blended Learning Framework for EFL Speaking Development
items.abstract: While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as conversational chatbots and speech recognition systems are increasingly adopted in language education, existing research focuses predominantly on isolated tools rather than integrated instructional models. This study proposes and evaluates a Human–AI Collaborative Blended Learning Framework for the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking skills. Using a two-phase research design, the study first synthesizes contemporary literature to establish a 7-layer conceptual framework that connects stakeholder participation, learner profiling, a Human–AI collaboration engine, blended activities, adaptive speaking services, teacher facilitation, and continuous learning analytics. Second, the framework was evaluated through an expert validation survey involving 52 specialists in language education, applied linguistics, and educational technology (40.4% PhDs, 57.7% Master’s). Quantitative findings revealed strong endorsement for actionable teacher support dashboards (80.8% agreement), visual pronunciation feedback (78.8%), and private AI speaking practice for anxiety reduction (75.0%; M = 2.98/4.00). However, experts expressed reservations regarding automated prompts for language elaboration (53.8% agreement), fixed 14-meeting schedules (57.7%), and automated grading weights (57.7%). Qualitative analysis highlighted that acceptance remains conditional upon accent fairness, data privacy, and active teacher oversight. Implications: Theoretically, the study advances AI-assisted language learning by establishing a human-centered collaborative model that prioritizes teacher-AI shared regulation over technological substitution. Pedagogically and practically, the findings imply that institutions and EdTech developers should deploy AI primarily for scalable, low-stakes rehearsal and actionable lesson planning, while preserving teacher authority over social communication, pragmatic competence, and high-stakes assessment.

items.title: Designing and Evaluating a Clinical Decision Support System to Assess Mild Cognitive Impairment
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly used in clinical decision support systems (CDSS) to improve the interpretability and trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions in healthcare. While prior work has examined how healthcare professionals (HCPs) interpret various explanation methods, limited research has investigated how these explanations function in systems that incorporate novel data sources like game-based digital biomarkers. This paper extends our previous work by presenting an improved, interactive web-based CDSS designed to support HCPs in assessing the risk of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). The system integrates ML predictions from gameplay data with data-centric, feature-importance, and counterfactual explanations to assist diagnosis and case-finding. We conducted a mixed-methods study with 51 HCPs to evaluate the system's understandability (objective and perceived), perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and trust. Participants gave consistently positive ratings across the self-reported perceived constructs, which were found to be strongly correlated. HCPs generally perceived the explanations as useful for clinical reasoning and reported that they understood and trusted the system, while acknowledging an initial learning curve. However, the evaluation of objective understanding was more mixed and correlated only weakly with the perceived constructs. In particular, participants encountered challenges in understanding game-based digital biomarkers, interpreting feature importances, combining local and global explanations, and understanding details of the underlying ML models. These findings highlight the importance of explanation designs that foster both positive user perceptions and accurate comprehension.

items.title: Designing The Post-Labor City: A Preliminary Inquiry Into The Conditions Of Cultural Generativity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may change the organization of productive labor without determining the distribution of resources, discretionary time, or cultural opportunities. This paper develops an interdisciplinary research landscape for examining post-labor urban possibilities under divergent technological and institutional conditions. The central question concerns how built environments, material provision, historical continuity, and governance shape the capacity of heterogeneous subjects to initiate, sustain, reinterpret, and revise meaningful relations. The inquiry distinguishes spatial access from effective participation; encounters from experienced meaning; valuation from institutional recognition; and immediate benefits from their consequences across historical trajectories. It connects task-based labor theories, monetary coordination, urban design, cultural policy, heritage scholarship, theories of power and justice, and ecological assessment without collapsing their distinct evidentiary standards. A generative–relational perspective is developed through the study of changing permissions, resources, relationships, and rights of revision. Its explanatory contribution is tested against existing accounts of capabilities, markets, urban morphology, institutional selection, and environmental impact. Comparative scenarios address commercial streets, pedestrian regimes, historical transmission, civic digital systems, and computational infrastructure. They specify candidate mechanisms, rival explanations, affected and absent participants, temporal horizons, and the limits of observation. The resulting research programme treats cultural generativity as a historically situated possibility whose significance requires plural empirical, interpretive, and normative evidence. It identifies the conditions under which urban interventions may expand participation, preserve living continuities, redistribute institutional power, and sustain ecological relations, while keeping future research and public judgment open to revision.

items.title: Determinants of (over)use and de-implementation of low-value infection prevention practices and care procedures that carry infection risks in hospitals: a scoping review
items.abstract: Introduction Infection prevention (IP) practices are critical to patient safety. However, some IP measures or care procedures associated with a risk of infection are used inappropriately or excessively. This overuse can be considered low-value care (LVC) as it contributes to potential negative health outcomes for patients, unnecessary healthcare costs, and environmental strain. This scoping review aims to identify determinants of (over)use and de-implementation of LVC general IP measures and non-surgical care practices linked to infection risk in hospitals. Methods We conducted a scoping review following Arksey and O’Malley methodology. A systematic search was performed in OVID/Medline, Embase.com, Elsevier/Scopus, and Ebsco/CINAHL up to January 29-February 2, 2026. Study selection was supported by the artificial intelligence tool ASReview using the SAFE-procedure. Data was charted using a piloted extraction form including type of study, type of LVC practice, and determinants of (over)use or de-implementation. Determinants were categorized according to Augustsson's de-implementation framework. Results A total of 13,738 records were retrieved of which 57 studies were included. Most included studies were empirical and focused on care procedures with an infection risk ( n = 40), predominantly urinary catheter use ( n = 37). Other studies addressed general IP measures ( n = 17), mainly glove use, sometimes combined with gowns/aprons ( n = 5) with two studies also including isolation practices. Across studies, determinants mainly related to professional-, patient-, and inner-context, and were primarily associated with continued (over)use rather than de-implementation. Many studies described situations of (over)use rather than explicitly probing the underlying motivations driving these behaviors. None of the studies explicitly labeled the examined care practices as LVC, and several did not specify criteria that distinguished appropriate from inappropriate use. Conclusions Current literature on determinants of (over)use and de-implementation in infection prevention focuses predominantly on urinary catheter and glove use, with a strong emphasis on determinants driving (over)use. Systematic study of overuse in infection prevention and subsequent development of effective de-implementation strategies is hindered by studies not clearly defining care practices as LVC. Advancing this field requires more theory informed and context-sensitive approaches to better characterize overuse, identify barriers and facilitators to reduce overuse, and to support the development of targeted de-implementation strategies.

items.title: DETERMINANTS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AMONG ACADEMIC AND NON-ACADEMIC STAFF OF AUCHI POLYTECHNIC, EDO STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined the determinants of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among academic and non-academic staff of Auchi Polytechnic, Edo State, Nigeria. Specifically, it investigated the relationships between perceived usefulness, AI literacy, institutional support and AI adoption. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 3,150 academic and non-academic staff, from which a sample of 354 respondents was determined using the Taro Yamane formula. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis with SPSS Version 26. The hypotheses were tested at the 5% level of significance. The descriptive results showed that perceived usefulness had a mean score of 4.18, AI literacy recorded 3.65, institutional support had 2.84, while AI adoption recorded 3.92. The multiple regression results indicated that perceived usefulness (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), AI literacy (β = 0.339, p < 0.001) and institutional support (β = 0.246, p < 0.001) had significant positive relationships with AI adoption. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F = 150.29, p < 0.001), with an R² of 0.545, indicating that the three explanatory variables jointly accounted for 54.5% of the variation in AI adoption. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor, followed by AI literacy and institutional support. The study concluded that AI adoption among staff of Auchi Polytechnic is associated with perceived work-related benefits, employees’ AI competencies and the availability of institutional resources and support. It recommended that the Polytechnic promote practical AI applications in academic and administrative activities, strengthen staff AI literacy through regular training, and improve digital infrastructure, technical assistance and institutional guidelines for responsible AI use.

items.title: Development and validation of scales to assess readiness for teaching among students in psychological and pedagogical profile classes
items.abstract: Introduction. The development of classes with a psychological-pedagogical focus emphasises the importance of the early identification of prerequisites for a teacher’s future professional development. At the pre-vocational stage, particular attention is given to the emerging moral, value-based, personal, and instrumental foundations necessary to foster readiness for pedagogical activity. However, contemporary psychological and pedagogical practice still lacks psychometrically validated diagnostic instruments capable of assessing students’ readiness for pedagogical activity in classes with a psychological-pedagogical focus. Aim . The present study aims to develop and pilot-test scales to assess students’ readiness for pedagogical activities in classes with a psychological and educational focus. Methodology and research methods. The methodological foundation of the study was the conceptualisation of readiness for pedagogical activity as a developing, multidimensional construct comprising moral-value, personal, and instrumental readiness. Based on a theoretical analysis, a bank of statements was created, which underwent expert evaluation and was discussed in a focus group with students. A total of 709 students in Years 10 and 11 (the final two years of secondary school), from classes with a psychological and pedagogical focus across ten regions of Russia, participated in the pilot testing of the developed scales. To verify the structure of the scales, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were employed; internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient; and convergent validity was evaluated through correlation analysis with indicators of motivation for choosing the teaching profession, adolescents’ professional attitudes, involvement in career guidance activities, and academic performance. Results. As a result of the study, three scales were developed to assess readiness for pedagogical activity at the pre-vocational stage. The scale of moral-value readiness comprises the indicators “Mission”, “Values”, and “Pragmatism”, which together account for 50.4% of the total variance. The scale of personal readiness includes the indicators “Identification”, “Self-regulation”, and “Independence”, explaining 46.2% of the total variance. The scale of instrumental readiness consists of the indicators “Experience”, “Difficulties”, and “Awareness”, accounting for 56.0% of the total variance. The internal consistency coefficients of the scale indicators range from 0.70 to 0.87. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed that the models fit the empirical data well. The χ²/df ratio did not exceed 2.73; Comparative Fit Index (CFI) values ranged from 0.946 to 0.961; Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI) from 0.925 to 0.948; Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) from 0.046 to 0.049; and Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) from 0.0395 to 0.0563. Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between the indicators of the readiness for pedagogical activity scales and confidence in professional choice, altruistic-intrinsic motivation, the influence of others, involvement in career guidance activities, and students’ academic performance. Scientific novelty. The study proposes and empirically tests a diagnostic instrument designed to assess readiness for pedagogical activity at the early, pre-vocational stage of developing the subject of pedagogical labour. The developed scales enhance understanding of school students’ readiness for pedagogical activity within the context of moral, value-based, personal, and instrumental prerequisites for future professional development in education. Practical significance. The findings may be utilised within systems of psychological and pedagogical support for students engaged in pedagogical activities, in designing targeted programmes to assist with professional self-determination, and in identifying various profiles related to the development of readiness for pedagogical work.

items.title: Differences in Translators' Cognitive Load under Generative-AI Post-Editing: An Eye-Tracking Study of English-Chinese Scientific Texts
items.abstract: {'en': 'Generative artificial intelligence has entered the translation workflow faster than evidence about its effect on the translator has accumulated. This study asks whether working from a large language model draft lowers cognitive load or merely redistributes it. Thirty-six translators, twenty translation trainees and sixteen practising professionals, rendered nine English popular-science and technical passages into Chinese under three within-subject conditions. These were unaided human translation (HT), post-editing of a static neural machine translation draft (NMT-PE), and post-editing of a GPT-4o draft with an interactive prompt pane (GAI-PE). Pupil diameter change, fixation duration, gaze distribution, keystroke logs, NASA-TLX ratings and MQM scores were recorded. GAI-PE cut task time by 44.2 per cent against HT and by 17.1 per cent against NMT-PE. Its MQM scores were higher than those of NMT-PE, while the difference from HT did not reach significance. Pupil diameter change was nevertheless largest in GAI-PE at 0.095 mm, against 0.083 mm in HT and 0.064 mm in NMT-PE, while gaze on the source text fell to 38.3 per cent, the lowest of the three. Subjective ratings moved the other way and ranked HT as the most demanding condition. In an exploratory analysis, self-reported AI-use frequency was associated with a smaller pupil response in GAI-PE, whereas English proficiency showed no such association. These observations are consistent with an increased demand for verification, though the generative condition also gave access to an interactive prompt pane, so the differences cannot be attributed to the model alone.'}

items.title: Differential Accuracy of Semantic Versus Phonological Speech Error Transcription in Aphasia: Comparing Large Language Model (Whisper) to Clinician (Speech-Language Pathologist) Performance
items.abstract: Purpose: Patient speech samples provide insights into cognitive and linguistic status, yet their utilization has been limited by labor-intensive manual transcription. Advances in automated speech recognition (ASR) with large language models (LLMs) potentially save time, but performance on impaired speech, such as due to poststroke aphasia, remains understudied. Method: We transcribed 4,535 trials of the Philadelphia Naming Test (PNT) administered to 26 people with aphasia (PWA) using OpenAI's Whisper speech-to-text LLM. These ASR transcripts were compared with gold-standard transcriptions by an experienced speech-language pathologist (SLP). Clinician–LLM match or mismatch in transcription was analyzed across speech-error types (semantic vs. phonemic), patient severities, and word frequency. Results: For each 175-trial PNT, transcriptions by SLP required 180 ± 40 min versus 2.3 ± 0.5 min by Whisper. Compared to > 95% match rate with SLP transcripts for trained humans, Whisper achieved an overall match rate of 75.52%, subdivided as 88.83% match on correct PNT trials, 92.22% on semantic errors, and 23.05% for trials with phonemic errors by PWA. Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient scores correlated with match rate ( R 2 = .196, p = .023) and hallucination rate ( R 2 = .291, p = .0048). Low-frequency words showed higher mismatch than medium- or high-frequency words (analysis of variance F = 14.26, p < .001). Conclusions: Whisper reliably transcribed semantic but not phonological errors, suggesting automation is best for fluent aphasia types with less phonemic distortions. This study benchmarks LLM transcription for impaired speech, offering a scalable alternative to manual transcription that may streamline clinical and research workflows. items.title: DIGITAL AND NEW WARFARE TECHNOLOGIES: PROTECTION OF HUMANITARIAN ASSETS IN CYBERWARFARE AND AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS SYSTEMS
items.abstract: The rapid development and deployment of digital and emerging technologies in armed conflict are transforming the nature, methods, and consequences of contemporary warfare. Cyber operations, artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous weapons systems (AWS), military robotics, satellite technologies, and other digitally enabled capabilities increasingly influence hostilities, while simultaneously creating unprecedented risks for civilians and humanitarian operations. This paper examines the legal and operational challenges arising from the use of digital and new warfare technologies, with particular emphasis on the protection of humanitarian assets in cyberwarfare and the regulation of autonomous weapons systems under IHL. This study investigates the extent to which the existing IHL framework, particularly the principles of distinction, proportionality, precautions in attack, military necessity, and protection of persons and objects indispensable to civilian survival, remains capable of addressing technologically mediated forms of warfare. Cyberattacks against hospitals, humanitarian organisations, water and electricity infrastructure, refugee facilities, humanitarian communication systems, digital health records and other assets upon which civilian populations and humanitarian actors depend. The paper also considers the challenges posed by the attribution of cyber operations, dual-use digital infrastructure, the classification of cyber operations as attacks, and the difficulties of applying traditional concepts of civilian objects and military objectives to interconnected digital networks. In relation to autonomous weapons systems, the study critically examines the implications of increasing machine autonomy for human control, accountability, and compliance with international human rights (IHL). This study considers whether existing legal rules are sufficient to regulate systems capable of selecting and engaging targets with limited or no direct human intervention, particularly where their operation may produce unpredictable or disproportionate effects. The paper further addresses questions of responsibility where harm results from autonomous decision-making and examines the relevance of weapons-review obligations under Article 36 of Additional Protocol I. The paper argues that technological developments do not displace the fundamental requirements of IHL; rather, they necessitate their careful application, clarification, and further development where appropriate. It advocates strengthened protection for humanitarian digital infrastructure, meaningful human control over the use of force, rigorous legal reviews of emerging weapons, improved international cooperation, clearer norms governing cyber operations during armed conflict, and effective mechanisms for accountability. The paper concludes that the preservation of humanitarian space in technologically mediated warfare requires an approach that combines existing international human rights (IHL) obligations with technologically informed regulatory standards capable of addressing the distinctive risks of cyberwarfare and autonomous weapons systems.

items.title: DIGITAL COMMUNISM IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: Artificial abundance, the devaluation of human labour, and the reconfiguration of economic value
items.abstract: The history of economics is inseparable from the evolution of the means of production. Every major technological transformation has altered the relationship between capital, labour, and the creation of wealth. Industrial mechanisation gradually replaced part of human physical effort with mechanical power. Computerisation subsequently automated many administrative, accounting, and information-processing operations. Today, generative artificial intelligence is introducing a different kind of rupture: it is directly involved in activities that traditionally relied on individuals’ cognitive, intellectual, and creative capacities. This transformation raises a fundamental question: what happens to the economic value of human labour when technologies make it possible to reproduce, accelerate, and standardise an increasingly large share of an individual’s productive capacities? The issue is not simply the possible disappearance of certain occupations. It concerns a deeper transformation in the mechanisms through which labour is valued. Artificial intelligence can substantially increase an individual’s productivity without guaranteeing a proportionate increase in remuneration. It may even reduce the market value of certain skills by making their use more accessible, faster, and less costly. We are therefore confronted with a paradox: individuals have access to increasingly powerful means of intellectual production, yet this increase in their productive capacity no longer necessarily secures them a stronger economic position. This contradiction is the starting point of our inquiry. We put forward the hypothesis that artificial intelligence is gradually separating three dimensions that were historically closely connected: the capacity to produce, the individual contribution to production, and the ability to capture a share of the wealth created. To analyse this transformation, we propose three organising concepts: digital communism, artificial abundance, and the tendency towards the devaluation of human labour. Our aim is not to argue that human labour is losing all economic usefulness, but to show that the conditions under which it is valued are changing. Value does not necessarily disappear: it shifts, becomes concentrated, and is recomposed.

items.title: Digital consciousness
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the emergence of digital consciousness through the interactions between consumers and intelligent technologies, drawing on Hoffman and Novak’s (2018) view that conscious experience arises from integrated interactions within a system. We explore how the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and emerging brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) reshape consumer experience by forming dynamic human–technology assemblages. Using assemblage theory (DeLanda, 2006; Deleuze & Guattari, 1987), we conceptualize consumer–object relationships as systems with emergent properties, where both human and non-human agents influence each other’s capacities and awareness. Three levels of experience—basic, aware, and conscious—are applied to both consumers and technologies, highlighting the potential (and limits) of artificial systems to develop forms of experiential processing. While deep integration technologies such as BCIs enhance agency, fusion, and symbiosis, they also raise concerns about automation, reduced conscious engagement, and ethical risks to identity, autonomy, and privacy. The chapter concludes by positioning digital consciousness as both an opportunity for personalized, embodied consumer well-being and a challenge demanding critical reflection on agency, transparency, and the ontological status of machine experience.

items.title: DIGITAL LABOUR AND EPISTEMIC ERASURE: A SEMIOTIC ANALYSIS OF INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND AI INFRASTRUCTURES IN HUMANS IN THE LOOP
items.abstract: This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures. The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.

items.title: Digital Technologies and Climate Change Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Emerging Trends and Research Directions
items.abstract: Abstract* Background Digital technologies offer new opportunities to support climate change education, yet the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and relationships between technological approaches, pedagogies, and educational objectives remain insufficiently characterized. This study maps the development of research on digital technologies for climate change education and identifies priorities for future investigation. Methods A bibliometric analysis was conducted using Scopus-indexed publications retrieved on 18 August 2026. The search strategy combined terms related to climate change education, climate literacy, and digital technologies. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 323 documents published between 2006 and 2026 were included. Bibliometrix and VOSviewer were used to examine publication characteristics, influential contributors, institutional and country contributions, scientific collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, thematic structure, and temporal research trends. Results The dataset comprised 323 documents from 179 publication sources, involving 1,141 authors. The analysis identified contributions from diverse institutions and countries, reflecting the interdisciplinary and internationally connected nature of the field. Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed seven thematic clusters encompassing climate literacy and public understanding; technological and experiential learning; computational and interdisciplinary learning; adaptation and sustainability; communication and place-based applications; technology-supported pedagogy; and curriculum and teacher capacity. The thematic and temporal analyses highlighted connections between digital technologies, pedagogical approaches, and climate-related educational objectives. However, the network structure indicates conceptual associations rather than demonstrated educational effectiveness. Potential research priorities include integrating digital technologies with systems thinking, strengthening pedagogical frameworks for immersive learning, investigating artificial intelligence in climate literacy, and evaluating learning transfer and sustained climate-related action. Conclusions This study provides a bibliometric overview of digital technology research in climate change education and identifies opportunities for more theoretically grounded and empirically robust investigation. Future research should combine explicit instructional designs with multidimensional learning assessments, longitudinal evaluation, and attention to teacher readiness and equitable technology access.

items.title: Digital Technology Use, Cognitive Engagement and Perceived Learning Effectiveness Among Adult Learners in Non-Formal Education in Uzbekistan
items.abstract: Abstract Although digital technologies are increasingly embedded in adult education policy, evidence from post-Soviet Central Asia remains scarce. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study examined how digital technology use relates to two proximal indicators of learning processes – cognitive engagement and perceived learning effectiveness – among adults in non-formal education programmes in Uzbekistan. Survey data from 312 learners nested in 26 programmes across three provinces were analysed with two-level random-intercept models, followed by semi-structured interviews with 22 learners and two facilitators, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. After adjustment for age, gender, educational attainment, urban–rural location and programme type, digital technology use was positively associated with cognitive engagement (β = .38, 95% CI [.27, .49]) and perceived learning effectiveness (β = .35, 95% CI [.24, .46]). Between 17% and 18% of the variance in each outcome lay at the programme level. Four qualitative themes – socially produced digital self-efficacy, peer-mediated learning, institutional culture and structural barriers – helped to explain these patterns. Interpreted through self-directed learning theory and the capability approach, the findings suggest that the educational value of digital tools depends on the social and institutional conditions in which adults use them. The cross-sectional design and reliance on self-report preclude causal inference.

items.title: Digital Transformation, Teaching Strategies, Critical Thinking, and Mathematics and Science Education
items.abstract: This issue focuses on digital transformation, teaching strategies, critical thinking, mathematics education, science education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on digital transformation. The articles examine Xuexitong for English learning, a component-based model of students' readiness to engage with digital platforms, the use of educational technology to enhance student performance in an English for Academic Purposes course, and the effectiveness of a distance teaching practicum program. Then, we present three articles on teaching strategies. The articles explore feminist pedagogy, the flipped classroom model, integration of humour into the classroom, and teacher effectiveness. We then share three articles on critical thinking. They investigate the Critical Thinking Assessment Scale-Short Form, embedding fiction in case studies within a non-literature course, and critical thinking skills. We continue with three articles on mathematics education. The articles examine integration of digital manipulatives in early childhood mathematics, Indonesia’s Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project, and student achievement. Then we present three articles on science education. They include articles on the effectiveness of guided inquiry, the impact of augmented reality learning, and the links between ethnoscience, science literacy, and digital literacy. We also present articles on race and racism, entrepreneurship education, professional learning communities, and academic calling. This issue includes two dialogue and commentary articles on Generative AI and large language models, concluding with four book reviews.

items.title: Digital transformation, traceability, and supply chain resilience in food manufacturing SMEs: a review of AI, blockchain-IoT, and institutional mechanisms
items.abstract: Food supply chains in China face persistent challenges of food safety risks, inadequate transparency, and supply disruptions, with food manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) disproportionately vulnerable due to limited resources and non-standardized internal processes. Digital transformation encompassing artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twin technologies is increasingly regarded as a strategic solution to strengthen supply chain resilience, yet the organizational and institutional conditions under which these digital investments translate into tangible resilience improvements for food manufacturing SMEs remain poorly understood. This review conducts a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and thematic synthesis of 40 multidisciplinary sources spanning the food safety, supply chain management, and information systems literatures. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Institutional Theory, we propose an integrative conceptual framework comprising six research propositions, in which traceability capability acts as a food-safety-specific mediating mechanism linking digital transformation to supply chain resilience, while regulatory stringency moderates the strength of this indirect pathway. A central argument of this framework is that deploying blockchain, IoT, or AI hardware does not itself constitute traceability capability the institutional and organisational conditions under which digital tools are adopted determine whether firms build substantive traceability capability or engage in symbolic compliance without genuine food safety governance improvement. Three key contributions distinguish this framework: conceptualizing traceability capability as a distinct dynamic capability rather than a generic digitalization mechanism; directing analytical focus explicitly toward food manufacturing SMEs, a population largely overlooked in existing large-firm panel studies; and introducing regulatory stringency as a first-stage moderator within a moderated mediation structure. Critical research gaps are identified, including the absence of SME-calibrated digital transformation measurement instruments, the lack of a validated multi-item traceability capability scale, and a complete empirical vacuum for testing the proposed moderated mediation model in food manufacturing SME contexts. This review provides a structured future research agenda for scholars and delivers actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers seeking to direct digital technology investments toward improved food safety governance in China’s food manufacturing sector.

items.title: DINOv3–SAM: Fusing Semantic and Anatomical Foundation Models for Robust Medical Image Classification
items.abstract: Abstract Robust medical image classification remains a persistent challenge due to heterogeneous acquisition protocols, label noise, and subtle inter-class variability. In chest radiography, these difficulties are compounded by shortcut learning from non-anatomical artifacts and projection variability, which severely undermine generalization. To address these limitations, we propose DINOv3–SAM, a dual-encoder framework that synergistically integrates complementary visual representations. The architecture combines a self-supervised DINOv3 vision transformer, which captures global semantic context, with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder, which provides anatomy-aware spatial features. The two feature streams are spatially aligned and adaptively refined through a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which emphasizes informative channels and diagnostically relevant regions prior to classification. Notably, only the final DINOv3 layers are fine-tuned while SAM remains frozen, yielding a computationally efficient framework with only 5.3 million trainable parameters. We evaluate DINOv3–SAM across five public datasets spanning diverse modalities and diagnostic tasks: pediatric pneumonia classification, cardiomegaly detection, large-scale RSNA pneumonia detection, COVID-19 radiography, and dermatological lesion classification. A unified stratified train/validation/test protocol ensures consistent and fair evaluation across both binary and multi-class settings. Each configuration was trained three times with different random seeds, and comprehensive comparisons against reproduced CNN baselines and published state-of-the-art methods, supported by statistical significance testing, demonstrate improvements across most datasets and metrics. The proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% (±3.06) on pediatric pneumonia, 97.24% (±0.77) accuracy (AUC 0.998 ±0.001) on COVID-19 radiography, and a mean AUC of 0.8705 (±0.0445) on the challenging RSNA benchmark. These results underscore the efficacy of fusing self-supervised semantic representations with segmentation-informed anatomical cues to enhance robustness against dataset bias, acquisition variability, and cross-domain shifts. The proposed approach offers a reliable foundation for multi-dataset and multi-modality medical image classification in research-oriented decision-support systems.

items.title: Discrete Memoryless Channel Capacity Estimation using Deep Learning and 256QAM
items.abstract: Abstract Channel capacity should be accurately estimated to design effective communication systems particularly in high-order modulation settings. In this paper, a deep learning-trained structure of the capacity estimation of discrete memoryless channels (DMCs) in the context of 256-Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (256QAM) is introduced. The presented approach is built upon Deep neural networks (DNNs) to train capacity directly based on input-output information, which is contrary to the classical methods like the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm which are both computationally intensive and depend on channel complexity. The simulation findings indicate that the CNN model has the capacity estimates that are close to the theoretical ones with low root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) at different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). The DNN-based capacity estimator takes 0.043 s (76% fast) to execute a test sample, which is much lower than the average execution time of the Blahut Arimoto algorithm of 0.184 s per SNR point, showing that the proposed approach is computationally efficient. The model is also more scalable and converges faster and hence can be used in real time applications. The article fits into the intersectional area of information theory and artificial intelligence, providing a viable and scalable capacity estimation methodology in next-generation wireless networks.

items.title: Divergent research orientations of affective and emotion concepts in artificial intelligence education through a bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Abstract This study employs bibliometric analysis to systematically review research trends in AI-driven affective and emotional education published in the Scopus database from 2020 to 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a dual-track keyword search strategy was adopted, ultimately yielding 401 documents for analysis. A five-dimensional coding framework was established encompassing research purpose, measurement channel, research participants, learning environment, and subject domain, with coding reliability confirmed through a triangulation procedure. Three principal findings emerged. First, keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed that the field has coalesced into four core clusters — technical recognition, psychological experimentation, specialized applications, and instructional practice — signaling that AI affective research has matured into a structurally coherent knowledge ecosystem. Second, longitudinal analysis identified 2023 as a critical inflection point: annual publication volume grew from 26 articles in 2022 to 197 in 2025, with the rise of generative AI driving a research shift from passive sensing and detection toward conversational affective scaffolding. Third, chi-square tests across all five research dimensions yielded statistically significant differences, confirming that "Affective" research is oriented toward educational practice while "Emotion" research is oriented toward technological development. This study proposes the Dual Knowledge Production Model of Affective and Emotion AI Research, clarifying the systematic academic division of labor between the two dominant terms and providing an empirically grounded framework to facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration.

items.title: Early prediction of post-dialysis systolic and diastolic blood pressure using intradialytic data in Senegalese hemodialysis patients: a single-center retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Intradialytic blood pressure variability poses a major challenge in chronic hemodialysis, especially in resource-limited settings, contributing to cardiovascular complications and session interruptions. This study aimed to develop and evaluate supervised machine learning models to predict post-dialysis systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) using only data available up to the third hour of the session. Methods In this retrospective, single-center cohort study at Hôpital Militaire Ouakam (Dakar, Senegal; February 2023 to November 2024), we analyzed 7,600 hemodialysis sessions from 124 chronic patients after quality-based exclusions. Predictors included intradialytic hemodynamics, dialysis machine parameters, and demographic and contextual factors recorded up to hour 3, while end-of-session data were excluded to prevent leakage. Four models were retained after initial screening of six candidates (Ridge Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost) and evaluated using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, with mean absolute error across SBP and DBP as the primary performance metric. Results Tree-based models outperformed linear and kernel-based methods, with the optimized Random Forest model achieving the best performance, with an MAE of 12.67 ± 0.80 mmHg for SBP and 8.93 ± 0.35 mmHg for DBP, a root mean square error of 14.68 ± 0.75 mmHg, and R² of 0.553 ± 0.033. Diastolic blood pressure predictions were more stable than systolic predictions, with no systematic bias observed in Bland-Altman analyses (bias = 0.015 mmHg for SBP and 0.395 mmHg for DBP). Subgroup performance showed moderate heterogeneity related to age, sex, and body mass index, with the best results observed in younger male patients. Conclusion These findings demonstrate the feasibility of supervised machine learning for unbiased prediction of post-dialysis blood pressure in Senegalese chronic hemodialysis patients, supporting the potential development of proactive interventions during hemodialysis sessions. Prospective and multicenter studies are needed to validate and measure the clinical impact of artificial intelligence use in the management of dialysis patients in resource-limited settings.

items.title: Emergency Response and Crisis Management
items.abstract: This chapter examines how AI is transforming emergency response and crisis management by strengthening emergency preparedness, communications, real-time coordination, and organizational resilience. Building upon the ESH Management System and PRIM governance framework introduced in earlier chapters, it demonstrates how AI enables organizations to shift from reactive emergency response to predictive, intelligence-driven preparedness. This chapter explores the application of machine learning, predictive analytics, computer vision, NLP, digital twins, IoT technologies, robotics, and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems to improve hazard detection, threat assessment, emergency planning, resource allocation, and decision-making. AI-supported emergency communications are presented as a means of delivering real-time, location-specific alerts, multilingual notifications, and coordinated situational awareness that improve response effectiveness during rapidly evolving events. This chapter also examines the role of robotics in hazardous and inaccessible environments, demonstrating how autonomous systems can support search and rescue, damage assessment, environmental monitoring, and post-incident recovery while reducing responder exposure to dangerous conditions. Real-world case studies, including British Petroleum’s Geospatial AI Engine and AI-assisted satellite analysis during the 2025 Myanmar earthquake response, illustrate how AI can accelerate damage assessment, improve operational coordination, and enhance emergency planning across both industrial and natural disaster settings. Collectively, these capabilities demonstrate how AI strengthens organizational preparedness, improves emergency response effectiveness, supports continual organizational learning, and enhances resilience within modern Emergency Preparedness Programs and crisis management systems.

items.title: Emerging Artificial Intelligence Applications in Capture Fisheries Monitoring and Assessment: A Bibliometric and Synthesis Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to monitor and assess capture fisheries, addressing persistent limitations of conventional observation systems that are labor‐intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. Despite rapid technological expansion, AI development in this field remains fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its structure and direction. This study aimed to map the development, intellectual structure, and thematic evolution of AI research in capture fisheries monitoring and assessment through a bibliometric and synthesis‐based review of Scopus‐indexed literature (2015–2026). Following a documented, large language model‐assisted screening protocol with human verification, a final corpus of 495 journal articles was analyzed using an integrated bibliometric and science‐mapping workflow. Results showed a marked, near‐exponential increase in publication output after 2020. Rather than confirming a pre‐defined three‐domain structure, keyword co‐occurrence analysis revealed that the field's thematic organization follows technical task type (detection, classification, and operational/vessel management) more closely than application domain, with acoustic AI failing to form an independent thematic cluster and representing the smallest share of the corpus (8.1%), behind visual AI (44.0%) and vessel monitoring (28.9%). For synthesis, we nonetheless compare the field across three functional categories visual AI for fish detection and measurement, vessel monitoring using AIS/VMS data, and acoustic survey support finding that the field is methodologically converging around a shared AI/ML toolkit while remaining largely siloed at the technical‐application level. Although research productivity remains heavily concentrated in China (85.9% of records) and international collaboration is limited (23.64%), the field is moving beyond isolated proof‐of‐concept studies toward more operational, management‐relevant applications. Overall, this study provides an evidence‐grounded, rather than assumed, understanding of how AI research in capture fisheries is thematically structured, and identifies acoustic AI and cross‐domain integration as priority areas for future development toward fisheries‐oriented, evidence‐based management.

items.title: Emerging Role of Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical QC and QA and its Applications across the Industry
items.abstract: Quality Control (QC) and Quality Assurance (QA) are key elements in the pharmaceutical sector. They help to ensure the safety, efficacy and consistency of medicines. This article discusses the purpose of QC and QA for pharmaceutical manufacturing in the modern era and outlines their development, principles and problems relating to the application of technology and universal quality standards. The article reaffirms the need for continuous and seamless improvement in the maintenance of quality system improvements that are responsible for global health standards and that can be applied to licensed drugs in a wide range of settings, ensuring the effectiveness of medicines delivered to patients in a sustainable manner. QC and QA are important components in pharmaceutical production. Their combined function is to ensure that all products are safe, efficient and reliable. As the industry evolves and moves toward digitalization, automation and data-centric systems, QC and QA evolve from reactive functions to predictive and preventive tools. Continuous improvements, regulatory compliance and the adoption of technology will shape the future of pharmaceutical quality. This paper also analyzes the beneficial use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the pharmaceutical sector throughout all phases, from drug discovery to drug development, as well as in various departments. Besides necessitating less human labor, it also improves the efficacy of clinical research and pharmaceutical output while diminishing the likelihood of mistake. The report examines the existing challenges in the implementation of AI within the pharmaceutical sector. Furthermore, it evaluates existing challenges and proposes remedies.

items.title: Emerging trends in pharmacovigilance: global surveillance systems, signal detection, risk assessment and patient safety
items.abstract: Pharmacovigilance has evolved from a system based mainly on spontaneous adverse drug reaction reporting into a multidimensional discipline that combines global case-report databases, active surveillance, pharmacoepidemiology, digital health records, patient-generated information and advanced analytics. This expansion is necessary because pre-authorisation trials cannot fully identify rare, delayed, interaction-related or population-specific harms that emerge during routine use. This narrative review examines the architecture of international pharmacovigilance, major surveillance platforms, signal-detection approaches, clinical and regulatory risk assessment, and current developments in artificial intelligence and real-world evidence. The World Health Organization Programme for International Drug Monitoring and VigiBase provide a framework for cross-national learning, while regional and national systems such as EudraVigilance, the United States Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System and India's Pharmacovigilance Programme of India support local reporting and regulatory action. Disproportionality methods, including the reporting odds ratio, proportional reporting ratio, information component and empirical Bayes approaches, are useful screening tools but do not establish causality or incidence. Active surveillance and well-designed non-interventional studies can strengthen signal evaluation by supplying denominators, comparators and longitudinal outcomes. Artificial intelligence can assist case processing, coding, duplicate detection and pattern recognition; however, biased data, limited external validation, weak explainability and automation errors require human oversight. Recent ICH E2D (R1) and M14 guidance further emphasise fit-for-purpose safety data and harmonised study methods. The review concludes that effective pharmacovigilance depends not on data volume alone but on reliable reporting, transparent analysis, timely risk communication, equitable global participation and practical measures that improve patient outcomes.

items.title: Empathy-driven remote pedagogy in accounting education − a bilingual model for student engagement and digital resilience
items.abstract: Purpose This paper presents the empathy-based bilingual digital pedagogy (EBBDP) model, a practice-informed framework developed through the author’s experience in remote teaching of accounting and taxation during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. It aims to show how pedagogical empathy can be translated into bilingual and digitally supported teaching practices intended to strengthen engagement, accessibility and emotional safety in virtual learning environments, particularly within technical education. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a reflective-practice methodology grounded in lived teaching experience within Portuguese vocational and professional training. It draws on pedagogical documentation, autoethnographic reflection and iterative adaptation of instructional strategies. The model integrates empathy, bilingual inclusivity and digital co-creation as central pedagogical pillars, illustrated through concrete examples using tools such as Google Workspace, Canva, Padlet and ChatGPT to support collaborative learning and formative assessment. Findings The reflective analysis identifies structured emotional check-ins, bilingual scaffolding, digital co-creation and multimodal assessment as practices through which pedagogical empathy may support accessibility, belonging and sustained participation. These practice-based interpretations are presented as conceptual propositions for future empirical testing rather than as measured effects. Originality/value This paper contributes to post-pandemic digital pedagogy by positioning empathy as a core teaching competence rather than a soft skill. It offers a conceptually grounded yet practice-driven model that translates pedagogical empathy into a structured set of bilingual, relational and digitally supported teaching practices, thereby bridging theory and classroom experience in technical education.

items.title: Enhancing Infrastructure Resilience Through Integrated Health, Safety and Environmental Risk Management in Saudi Arabia's Industrial Projects
items.abstract: Industrial infrastructure in Saudi Arabia is undergoing expansion and renewal with the environment being as much a factor as the infrastructure itself with exposure to extreme heat, flash flooding, complex supply chains and highly interdependent utility services. Traditional HSE (health, safety and environment) arrangements will only go some way towards reducing the number of discrete incidents and will not in any way guarantee the continued function of the essential infrastructure in the face of a compound disruption. This is a critical integrative review of how occupational health, process safety, environmental protection and asset resilience can be managed as one decision system across the industrial project lifecycle. A total of 30 peer reviewed papers published between 2020 and 2025 were purposefully selected for this study, including three which were specifically Saudi focused. These were subjected to a thematic analysis looking at hazard pathways, institutional controls, operational dependencies and recovery capabilities. The synthesis of the findings identifies five persistent disconnects: compliance at the project level versus continuity at the network level; metrics of occupational injury versus metrics of major accident precursors; environmental assessment versus operational safeguards; information gathering versus accountable decisions; and controls in the construction phase versus controls for long term adaptation. In response to these disconnects the paper proposes an integrated resilience governance model which links critical function mapping, dynamic HSE risk assessment, protective barriers, cross operator coordination and performance based learning. Indicators are specified to support the model but are not presented as validated field thresholds. The contribution of this work is a testable management architecture rather than a claim of any measured national performance. It provides a framework which could be used by owners, regulators and delivery partners to help prioritise the interventions that will jointly protect workers, communities, the environment and the continued function of the key services.

items.title: Enhancing the accessibility of population-based cancer screening: insights from co-creation on a screening portal and a combined screening programme
items.abstract: Introduction Population-based cancer screening programmes facilitate early cancer detection, thereby contributing to reduced cancer-related morbidity and mortality. However, participation rates have declined in recent years, with lower uptake particularly evident among invitees in vulnerable positions. This decline can be partly attributed to information that is insufficiently tailored to individual needs and literacy levels, and to the fragmented nature of the screening offer. To address these barriers, this study explored two strategies: (1) developing a personalised screening portal presenting information in an accessible and tailored manner, and (2) improving the alignment and potential integration of screening programmes. Methods Four co-creation sessions were conducted with 13 screening invitees and eight experts in cancer screening and human factors engineering. Two sessions focused on prototyping a screening portal and two explored the potential for combined screening. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed thematically using inductive coding. Results Invitees and experts emphasised the need for a digital portal offering concise, empathetic, personalised, and phase-specific information. Invitees perceived added value in combined screening, whereas experts considered organising all screenings at a single location and time to be infeasible in the current context. Both groups agreed that integrating information provision across programmes would be valuable and feasible. Discussion These findings suggest that integrating information across screening programmes is a meaningful and achievable step towards improving accessibility and supporting informed decision-making, particularly for invitees in vulnerable positions.

items.title: Environmental, Safety, and Health Artificial Intelligence Implementation Strategies and Challenges
items.abstract: This concluding chapter presents a practical roadmap for implementing AI within an ESH Management System by integrating project management, governance, organizational change, and continual improvement into a unified implementation strategy. Building upon the PRIM framework developed throughout the book, this chapter demonstrates how organizations can systematically acquire, deploy, govern, and sustain AI technologies while minimizing operational, regulatory, and organizational risks. It examines the application of established project management principles, including scope, cost, schedule, and risk management, together with a structured example illustrating how PRIM can guide AI model acquisition and implementation. This chapter introduces the PRIM AI Maturity Model as a governance framework for assessing organizational readiness and advancing AI integration from initial experimentation to optimized, continuously improving capabilities. Recognizing that successful AI adoption depends as much on people as technology, this chapter explores change management, workforce training, communication strategies, and the Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability Reinforcement (ADKAR) model to foster employee trust, competency, and organizational acceptance. It also addresses AI records management, regulatory compliance, ethical considerations, transparency, and accountability as essential components of responsible AI governance. Finally, this chapter examines the influence of AI on organizational culture, emphasizing that sustainable transformation requires leadership commitment, ethical decision-making, and continual learning. Collectively, the concepts presented throughout this chapter reinforce the central theme of the book that AI achieves its greatest value when governed through the PRIM framework and embedded within a mature ESH Management System, where technology, governance, leadership, and organizational culture work together to improve worker safety, environmental stewardship, operational resilience, and long-term organizational excellence.

items.title: Environmental, Safety, and Health Management Basics
items.abstract: This chapter establishes the foundational principles of Environmental, Safety, and Health (ESH) Management and introduces the essential concepts that underpin the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern ESH practice. It distinguishes between individual ESH Programs and an integrated ESH Management System, demonstrating how management systems provide a structured, risk-based framework for governance, regulatory compliance, continual improvement, and organizational performance. This chapter examines the roles of leadership, organizational culture, worker commitment, and systematic issue management in creating effective ESH Programs while emphasizing internationally recognized management system standards, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14001 and ISO 45001. It also introduces the principles of risk management, including hazard identification, risk assessment, prioritization, mitigation, monitoring, and continual reassessment, as fundamental components of an effective ESH strategy. Together, these concepts provide the organizational and technical foundation necessary for understanding how AI can responsibly enhance hazard recognition, decision-making, predictive analytics, compliance, and overall ESH performance throughout the remainder of the book.

items.title: Epigenetic Sustainability: Modeling the Human Factor as a Natural Resource through Science 4.0 and the NR3C1 Biological Pilot
items.abstract: Traditional industrial and organizational paradigms treat human capital as an elastic, indefinitely renewable asset. However, under chronic operational strain, biological systems undergo progressive, non-linear degradation governed by thermodynamic and epigenetic constraints. Within the Science 4.0 framework, this paper formulates the “Human Factor” as an exhaustible, dissipative natural resource operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium. We introduce a conceptual non-equilibrium thermodynamic model that relates chronic socio-technical load to increased biological dissipative demand and internal entropy production (σ_ent), challenging the organism’s buffering capacity. To explore this framework at the molecular interface, we deploy the Nuclear Receptor Subfamily 3 Group C Member 1 ( _NR3C1_ ) gene as an illustrative biological pilot. We model how sustained operational strain relates to cumulative allostatic load and context-dependent epigenetic remodeling at the _NR3C1_ promoter (exon 1F), which in some experimental and clinical contexts has been associated with attenuated glucocorticoid receptor expression, represented within the model as a reduction in the normalized Bioenergetic Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR*_bio). Using a Shannon-inspired informational capacity formulation, we analyze the conditions under which homeostatic feedback loops lose fidelity. Modeling the human factor through thermodynamic and kinetic resource-depletion curves provides a hypothesis-generating foundation for sustainable ergonomics, regenerative governance, and the preservation of biological integrity in high-demand socio-technical architectures.

items.title: Essential but vulnerable: a model for understanding how macro–meso–micro-level factors combine to impede the sustainability of female health providers
items.abstract: Purpose Global health discourse has increasingly focused on achieving universal health coverage, yet the occupational health needs of the workforce delivering these services remain systematically neglected. This paper aims to address the systematic neglect of the occupational health needs of female health-care providers – principally nurses and midwives – in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The paper makes particular reference to Sub-Saharan Africa. It develops an integrative multilevel conceptual model that explains how this neglect is produced, transmitted and amplified and proposes implementable multilevel responses. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a structured integrative literature review, reported in line with the PRISMA 2020 statement, and conducted for the purpose of conceptual model development. Eighty-six sources retained from six databases and grey literature repositories were synthesised through a codebook-style thematic analysis. It draws on the Social Determinants of Health (SDH) framework, Moral Injury Theory, the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model and the Health Equity Framework. Findings The synthesis suggests that macro-level structural determinants are proposed to produce the foundational architecture of provider neglect. Meso-level organisational factors are proposed to transmit macro-structural neglect into the lived realities of individual providers. Micro-level clinical stressors appear to amplify the intermediate consequences experienced by individual providers beyond what structural and organisational factors alone imply. Gendered structures operate as a cross-cutting context conditioning every level of the model. Feedback loops link deteriorating health system outcomes back to macro- and meso-level conditions. Dismantling provider neglect is therefore proposed to require simultaneous interventions at all three levels of the model. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual paper, the proposed model is not empirically tested. It requires empirical validation through quantitative and qualitative studies across different health-care settings, particularly in LMICs. Cross-national comparative studies across Sub-Saharan African, South Asian and Latin American contexts would test the model’s generalisability. Longitudinal studies tracking the same provider cohorts over time would help examine the proposed sequence and feedback loops. Practical implications The paper emphasises the necessity for national governments, health ministries and institutions and policymakers to establish comprehensive occupational health programmes, dedicated health insurance schemes for providers, workplace wellness initiatives, mental health services and financial protection mechanisms. It specifies responsible actors, implementation priorities and measurable outcomes for each recommendation. International development partners, global health donors and multilateral organisations should integrate health-care workforce welfare into health systems-strengthening investments. Social implications The study reframes health-care providers as a vulnerable population whose health needs are often overlooked within health-care systems. It contributes to sustainable development goals 1 (end poverty in all its forms everywhere), 3 (ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all), 8 (productive employment and decent work and economic development for all), 10 (reduce inequality) and 16 (provide access to justice for all). Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study to integrate macro-, meso- and micro-level explanations of health-care provider neglect within a single conceptual model that embeds gender-specific mechanisms and feedback loops in its connecting structure. It reframes this neglect as an equity and social justice issue rather than a management problem. It extends Moral Injury Theory into the domain of occupational health exclusion. It repositions the SDH framework as a tool for analysing occupational health inequalities among the health workforce itself.

items.title: Ethical Implications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use Among Library and Information Science (LIS) Students: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by students and is reshaping the way information is accessed, processed, and utilised for academic work and everyday purposes. As the use of AI technologies continues to expand, there is a growing need to discuss the ethical implications associated with the use of generative AI among LIS students. This study employed a narrative review method to analyse and synthesise evidence from existing scholarly literature obtained through various library resources and online databases on the Internet. The study identified several ethical implications regarding the use of generative AI among LIS students, which include breaches of academic integrity, plagiarism risks, misinformation, output bias, privacy and security concerns, reduced critical engagement with learning materials, overdependence on AI systems, fabricated references, and so on. The findings revealed that ethical use of generative AI requires LIS students to critically evaluate AI-generated content, acknowledge AI assistance where necessary, and maintain responsibility for the accuracy and originality of their academic work. The study showed areas for future research directions in ethical concerns of generative AI use among LIS students for responsible AI use in academic practices.

items.title: EVALUATING THE ACCURACY AND RELIABILITY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CHATBOTS IN ANSWERING DENTAL SPECIALTY EXAMINATION PERIODONTOLOGY QUESTIONS
items.abstract: Background/Aim: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized by dental students and specialty candidates as supplementary tools for examination preparation. However, their reliability in specialized clinical domains requiring analytical reasoning remains underexplored. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and inter-model agreement of three contemporary reasoning-focused LLMs in answering Periodontology questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DUS).Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional in silico study, 100 multiple-choice Periodontology questions administered in past DUS sessions (2012–2026) were selected. The questions were presented in isolated sessions without prior contextual prompting to three models: OpenAI GPT-5.5 Thinking, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 (adaptive thinking), and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro. Responses were scored dichotomously against official answer keys. Overall accuracy rates were compared using Cochran's Q test, pairwise agreement was assessed via Cohen's Kappa (k) coefficient, and shared error distributions were analyzed using a two-tailed Binomial test (p 0.05), ChatGPT and Gemini selected the identical incorrect distractor in all 5 questions they mutually failed (100% shared error rate; p = 0.0625).Conclusion: Contemporary reasoning-capable LLMs demonstrate high accuracy and substantial inter-model consistency on specialty-level Periodontology questions. Nevertheless, the presence of concordant errors indicates shared algorithmic blind spots, underscoring that AI outputs must be supplemented by specialist oversight and evidence-based verification in dental education.

items.title: Evaluating the AI-predictive potential of the PIC database for pediatric ICU mortality
items.abstract: Abstract Background Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research. Methods This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior. Results ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea. Conclusion Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models. Impact Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling. Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance. Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators. Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.

items.title: Evaluating the Validity of AI-Generated Writing Feedback for Students With Learning Disabilities
items.abstract: Students with learning disabilities need clear, direct, and useful writing feedback. However, teachers often find it hard to provide this consistently because of time and workload pressures. New developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) might help improve both the frequency and quality of feedback for students. Still, we know very little about whether AI-generated comments are valid or useful for struggling writers. This qualitative study looked at teachers' views on writing feedback from the AI-SCORE automated writing evaluation tool. Nine upper elementary and middle school teachers took part in two focus groups. They reviewed AI-generated feedback on student informational writing. They also discussed its clarity, teaching value, and suitability for students with disabilities. Thematic analysis revealed several areas for improving AI-generated feedback. Teachers want more guidance on specific revisions, language that suits students’ development, a consistent tone, and alignment with writing goals. They shared cautious optimism, noting that AI feedback could enhance teaching capacity and provide more practice opportunities for students, if it meets their needs. The findings stress the importance of teacher involvement, the potential benefits of AI for writing instruction, and key factors for creating AI tools that effectively support students with learning disabilities.
