items.title: Evaluation of Clinical and Theoretical Knowledge of Scaling and Root Planing in Northern Brazil Dental Schools
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Scaling and root planing (SRP) is traditionally the initial therapy in the treatment of periodontitis. So, clinicians should develop a solid theoretical knowledge of instrumentation and the required clinical skills. This study aimed to evaluate the educational exposure, pedagogical perceptions, and the level of clinical and technical knowledge of undergraduate dental students regarding SRP to identify knowledge gaps. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and August 2025 with 105 students distributed into G1 (1st-3rd semester), G2 (4th-7th semester) and G3 (8th-10th semester). Data were collected using a digital form containing epidemiological and technical questions in dichotomous and multiple-choice formats, addressing identification of periodontal instruments, specific clinical indications for SRP instruments, operative principles, post-SRP clinical effects, grasp techniques and professional-patient ergonomics. Statistical analyses were performed using Chi-square and G tests (p ≤ 0.05). RESULTS: Significant differences in theoretical and practical exposure to SRP were observed (p < 0.0001). Technical performance demonstrated significant knowledge gaps; for instance, only 63.8% correctly identified Gracey curettes, and approximately half demonstrated mastery over sickle scalers (52.4%) and less than half for hoes (46.7%). There were significant differences among groups in distinguishing between surgical and non-surgical instruments (p < 0.0001). A deficit in operative skills was noted, particularly in professional-patient ergonomics, with 53.3% correct answers, and in grasp technique, with a correct response rate of 6.7%, indicating gaps in preclinical psychomotor training. CONCLUSION: The study reveals potential gaps in the retention of technical-scientific knowledge among students, suggesting that exploring continuous reinforcement strategies may benefit the teaching of scaling and root planing in northern Brazilian dental schools.

items.title: Existential Self-Perception In Post-Labor Societies
items.abstract: Extensive delegation of productive and intellectual activities to artificial intelligence may reconfigure the conditions under which people encounter tasks, develop purposes, and interpret their participation. This paper investigates existential self-perception through the distinction between external outcomes and the relational histories of their production and experience. It differentiates ontological existence, prereflective ownership, experienced agency, narrative continuity, interpersonal recognition, and institutional standing. Its central proposition concerns the distribution of experiential participation: AI mediation can alter access to intermediate decisions, resistance, feedback, and revision, even when the resulting output remains comparable. The analysis extends this proposition to the development of purposes, ecological and aesthetic encounters, absorbed attention, and the temporal organization of habits and recollection. It proposes conditional tests of the relational-feedback account while considering output quality, novelty, task demands, and material conditions as competing influences. Meaningful participation can occur with reduced explicit self-monitoring, while the significance of an episode may develop through subsequent relationships and reflection. A complementary research program proposes episode-level elicitation, bounded comparisons of delegation, longitudinal observations, and studies of shared environments. These designs distinguish experiential reports, observable activity histories, and institutional conditions, enabling investigation of how different arrangements of delegation shape opportunities for participation. The post-labor counterfactual provides a setting for examining diverse experiences and forms of self-understanding amid changes in productive necessity.

items.abstract: Background Accurate identification of primary suspect drugs in adverse event reports is a critical component of post-marketing pharmacovigilance and serves as a foundation for downstream signal detection activities. However, causal attribution in spontaneous reporting systems such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is inherently challenging. Traditional expert-based assessments are resource-intensive and difficult to scale, highlighting the need for complementary, reproducible approaches. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of large language models (LLMs) in identifying primary suspect drugs in adverse event reports against an expert reference standard. Methods Fifty FAERS case reports were randomly selected for evaluation. Three clinical pharmacy experts established the reference standard by adjudicating the primary suspect drug(s) for each case. LLM-based evaluations were conducted using multiple prompting strategies and model configurations. The performance of LLMs, pharmacy student evaluators, and original FAERS primary suspect designations (ROLE_COD) was assessed by calculating hit rates against the expert reference standard. Results The original FAERS designations demonstrated limited accuracy against the expert reference standard, with a hit rate of 0.778. In contrast, LLM-based assessments achieved consistently high hit rates ranging from 0.867 to 0.920 across diverse prompting strategies and model configurations. Student evaluators achieved a comparable hit rate of 0.872; however, LLM-based evaluations exhibited greater internal consistency and markedly shorter response times. Conclusion LLM-based evaluations demonstrated high accuracy against expert assessments and favorable efficiency relative to student evaluators. These findings highlight the potential utility of LLMs as scalable, readily accessible decision-support tools in pharmacovigilance workflows.

items.title: Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Contrastive Learning for Electricity Theft Detection in Smart Grids (SSTCL-AD-XAI)
items.abstract: Abstract Electricity theft imposes substantial revenue losses on utility operators and threatens smart-grid stability. Existing detection methods struggle with scarce labelled anomalies, distribution shift, and opaque decision boundaries that hinder forensic auditing. This paper proposes SSTCL-AD-XAI, a self-supervised temporal contrastive learning framework with explainable artificial intelligence for anomaly detection in hourly electricity consumption data. A two-layer LSTM encoder is first pre-trained via InfoNCE contrastive loss with stochastic augmentations — random hour masking, multiplicative scaling, and additive Gaussian noise — and then fine-tuned with Focal Loss under a leakage-safe protocol in which validation data serve only for model and threshold selection. Evaluated on a combined synthetic and SGCC corpus of 42,872 samples over 10 independent seeds, the framework attains a mean F1-score of 0.914, a mean ROC-AUC of 0.975, and a mean PR-AUC of 0.949. It significantly outperforms six unsupervised detectors — LOF, One-Class SVM, HBOS, Deep Autoencoder, DAGMM-like Autoencoder, and Transformer Autoencoder — at Wilcoxon p=0.002, and exceeds a supervised BiLSTM reference in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC while matching its F1-score. Source-wise evaluation confirms that performance is carried by the real SGCC data (SGCC-only F1 0.914), and a 5% prevalence stress test quantifies the deployment operating point (Recall 0.955, Precision 0.357). Multi-seed ablation identifies self-supervised pre-training as the dominant performance driver. Sequence-aware attribution via Integrated Gradients and temporal occlusion, computed exclusively on SGCC samples, confirms midnight consumption (H1) as the most discriminative forensic feature, and quantitative embedding metrics (silhouette 0.548; Davies-Bouldin 0.786) verify moderate and consistent class structure. The framework demonstrates promising potential for transparent electricity theft detection and provides a foundation for future validation in operational smart-grid environments.

items.title: Exploring AI as a reading companion: L2 learners' approaches to literary comprehension
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI tools are increasingly present in language learning, yet their role in second language (L2) reading remains underexplored. This study investigates how intermediate German learners engaged with ChatGPT during interpretive reading using a three‐condition design with a Grimm fairytale. The study examines the relationship between AI access and reading performance, patterns of use or resistance, and students' ethical and motivational interpretations of AI‐mediated reading. Generative AI emerged as a negotiated presence that learners approached with curiosity, caution, or resistance. Required AI use was associated with reduced differences in comprehension outcomes across proficiency levels, whereas optional use revealed diverse strategic, reluctant, and value‐driven stances rooted in ethical concerns, discipline‐specific norms, and a desire to maintain interpretive autonomy. Students who routinely used AI in other courses engaged more selectively in German, suggesting AI practices may be shaped by disciplinary contexts. The findings support guided, reflective AI integration while valuing learner resistance.

items.title: Exploring Spatial Inequities and Livability: A Mixed-Methods Study Using Artificial Intelligence and Community Insights
items.abstract: Abstract Rapid urbanization has intensified health and social inequities through the uneven distribution of infrastructure, services, and public space. In St. Louis, Missouri (USA), these disparities remain geographically concentrated and rooted in long-standing patterns of racial segregation and disinvestment. This study examines how spatial inequities shape urban livability by integrating scalable artificial intelligence (AI) methods with community-based insights. We applied a vision–language model, supported by a large language model, to classify micro-scale built-environment features from 7,848 Google Street View segments, and conducted semi-structured interviews with residents and stakeholders. The AI analysis revealed baseline infrastructure such as street lighting (85%) and continuous pavements (77%), but very low coverage of universal-design features: curb ramps (9.7%), pedestrian crossings (7.1%), and walk signals (4.3%). These deficits were significantly associated with lower median incomes and higher proportions of non-Hispanic Black residents. Qualitative findings confirmed and contextualized these patterns, linking them to historical redlining, fragmented governance, and everyday experiences of constrained mobility and safety. By combining scalable AI tools with community narratives, this study demonstrates that spatial inequities are both visible in the physical streetscape and embodied in daily life. Methodologically, it advances the use of VLM and LLM-enabled pipelines for urban audits; conceptually, it reframes livability metrics through the lens of spatial equity; and practically, it provides a replicable framework for equity-centered planning.

items.abstract: Face presentation attacks threaten the dependability of facial biometric authentication, particularly when conventional RGB cameras are exposed to print and replay artefacts. Existing texture descriptors are computationally attractive but remain sensitive to noise, illumination variation, and image degradation, whereas many deep architectures require substantial data and processing resources. Prior studies establish the value of handcrafted texture features, Binary Statistical Image Features (BSIF), auxiliary-supervised networks, and foundation-model approaches, but the reviewed evidence does not explicitly assess Gaussian linear filtering as a face-image preprocessing stage before BSIF extraction. This study adopted is structured into sequential and interconnected phases were integrates Gaussian linear filter with sigma 1.0, eight-bit BSIF coding, a normalised 256-bin histogram, feature standardisation, and support vector classifier (SVC). Experiments use OULU-NPU, with five-fold validation on SiW and CASIA-FASD. On the reported OULU experiment, the system achieved 87.28% accuracy, 65.83% precision, 76.70% recall, a 70.85% F1-score, and 93.39% ROC-AUC, compared with 73.50% accuracy and 0.724 ROC-AUC for raw-pixel SVC. Mean accuracy was 83.69% on SiW and 95.05% on CASIA-FASD. Gaussian filter- BSIF features provide a compact and discriminative representation for software-only face presentation attack detection. The work demonstrates a lightweight preprocessing-texture-classification pipeline and reports both predictive and computational measures. Future studies should enhance the robustness, scalability, adaptability, and efficiency of face presentation attack detection by integrating advanced preprocessing techniques, multimodal biometrics, lightweight artificial intelligence models, and adaptive learning strategies.

items.title: Facilitating virtual design reviews: CAD and SysML model integration in virtual reality environments
items.abstract: Due to the integration of mechanical, electronical and software functions in modern products, virtual product development is becoming increasingly important. In this context, virtual prototyping in particular can benefit from the visualization of CAD models of a system in virtual reality (VR) simulations, as this can support activities such as ergonomic assessments and design reviews in the early stages of development. Furthermore, managing the growing complexity of products can be supported by creating consistent system models following the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach. By combining system models, created by SysML modeling syntax, CAD models, and VR simulations, benefits for the virtual model-based product development can be generated and information as well as model consistency can be improved. This article introduces a tool for the integration, simultaneously visualization, and automated linking of SysML and CAD models in an interactive VR environment. The tool can support design review and validation processes by displaying CAD objects and the associated information of the system model in one virtual environment at the same time. The focus of the exemplary tool application in this article is the validation of system requirements defined in a SysML model through the examination of a true-to-scale CAD model in VR. As a build-in feature, the validation results can be documented in the VR simulation and returned back to the SysML modeling tool so that they can be taken into account in further system development. The tool validation demonstrates potential for virtual reviews, early requirement validation, and bidirectional data exchange.

items.title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.

items.title: Fear of negative evaluation and technology-acceptance perceptions in human–AI interaction: a study on intelligent chat services
items.abstract: Fear of negative evaluation (FNE) is typically conceptualized as a concern about interpersonal judgment, but as artificial intelligence (AI) systems become more interactive, users may also anticipate evaluation from AI itself. This study examined whether FNE from humans (FNEH) and from AI (FNEA) are differentially associated with technology-acceptance perceptions. University students and faculty (N = 203) completed parallel measures of FNEH and FNEA, along with measures of perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and perceived enjoyment (PE) for intelligent chat services. Structural equation modeling showed that FNEH was negatively associated with PU and PE, whereas FNEA was negatively associated with PEOU and PE. The two PE associations did not remain significant after Holm adjustment. Direct comparisons showed that FNEH and FNEA differed significantly only for PEOU, with FNEA showing the stronger negative association. Their associations with PU and PE did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that the source of anticipated evaluation may be particularly relevant to perceived ease of interacting with AI. The study extends research on FNE to human–AI interaction and highlights the importance of examining evaluative concerns in users’ perceptions of AI-based technologies.

items.title: Feasibility of a Flipped Learning–Based Low Back Training Programme in Nurses to Support Ergonomic Knowledge, Performance, and Confidence
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Aims To evaluate the feasibility of a flipped learning low back training programme among nurses, focussing on ergonomic knowledge, exercise performance and confidence, and participant satisfaction. Background Work‐related low back pain is a common occupational health problem among nurses. Comprehensive training programs including promotion of ergonomic knowledge, proper exercise performance, and confidence may enhance safe musculoskeletal practice. Design Feasibility study. Methods Twenty registered nurses were recruited from a graduate nursing programme between 2022 and 2023 with prior clinical experience. The training programme used a flipped‐learning approach, incorporating evidence‐based low back exercises and gamified strategies. Meanwhile, ergonomic knowledge was assessed post‐programme and at 1‐year follow‐up, the exercise performance was rated during training and confidence in back exercise performance was self‐reported at follow‐up. Participant satisfaction was also measured. Results Participants demonstrated high ergonomic knowledge (mean score 71/100) after training, which remained satisfactory at 1‐year follow‐up (64.4/100). Peer scores of 13 low back exercises ranged from fair to excellent. Self‐confidence in performing the exercises 1 year later ranged from 7 to 9 out of 10, reflecting sustained ability to properly perform the exercises. Participants' satisfaction was high, indicating acceptance and perceived value in the programme. Conclusions The flipped learning–based low back training programme was feasible for nurses and supported retention of ergonomic knowledge, correct exercise performance, and sustained confidence 1 year after training. High participant satisfaction further supports its acceptability, suggesting its potential for future implementation in clinical musculoskeletal practice. These observations are exploratory given the descriptive study design; hence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

items.title: From Adoption to Human-AI Leadership: A Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Leadership and Management
items.abstract: This scoping review maps how artificial intelligence is conceptualized and used in educational leadership and management and examines the transition from technology adoption toward human-AI leadership. Following established scoping-review guidance and PRISMA-ScR, records from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed published or officially available online from 2022 to the final search date in 2026 were screened; items assigned a 2027 bibliographic year were eligible only if already available online before the cutoff. Of 747 records identified, 183 duplicates were removed and 323 records underwent title-and-abstract screening. Full texts were sought for 81 reports; two could not be retrieved, 79 were assessed for eligibility, and 50 studies were included. Four themes emerged: leadership readiness and capability; AI-augmented leadership practice; organizational conditions and institutional transformation; and human-AI agency, governance, and ethical boundaries. The evidence favors augmentation rather than autonomous substitution, with human judgment remaining central to accountability. The review proposes a five-stage Human-AI Educational Leadership Continuum integrating individual capability, organizational readiness, governance, and decision authority. The review was limited to three databases and English-language articles, and the evidence base remains methodologically heterogeneous and largely cross-sectional or context-specific.

items.title: From Charitable Waste to Sustainable Wellbeing: A Research Framework for Unused Qurbani Value and a Proposed "Smart Waqf Fund" Model
items.abstract: This working paper sets out a research framework for examining value that may go unused in the Qurbani (sacrificial animal) system, and a proposed "Smart Waqf Fund" model for governance, innovation and social development. It links Sharia grounding, operational governance, legal characterisation, economic feasibility and social development, and keeps established facts, research hypotheses and institutional proposals clearly separate. Part One sets out the framework: the institutional idea of preserving the asset and benefiting from its fruit; a six-stage method for measuring utilisation in the Qurbani chain; a proposed research farm; temporary cash waqf and waqf units; digital administration; the GoSmart knowledge alliance; human wellbeing; education through the Awqaf animal family; and a research roadmap. Part Two contains supporting research files on risk management, a preliminary comparison of seven jurisdictions (New Zealand, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, Kuwait, Bahrain and Malaysia), multilingual awareness and artificial intelligence, AAOIFI Governance Standards 14 and 15, the fiqh question of temporary cash waqf and qard hasan (pending before the 12th Forum on Waqf Fiqh Issues), economic feasibility, research and vocational training, and publication rights. Status: a developmental research working paper, open to critique. It is not peer reviewed and is not a fatwa, a legal opinion, an offer document or an invitation to participate financially. It reports no measured results. No waqf units are offered in any jurisdiction. All figures are editorial illustrations, not charts based on measured data. Two editions are deposited: the Arabic original and a full English translation, each as an A4 PDF. Licence note: published under CC BY-NC 4.0. The Awqaf New Zealand name and logo are excluded from the licence; third-party material, including AI-assisted illustrations, remains subject to its own terms.

items.title: From Communication Anxiety to Psychological Reliance
items.abstract: Abstract: Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how communication anxiety and psychological need satisfaction relate to the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, for communication tasks (e.g., writing emails, drafting messages, and preparing scripts). Using a three-wave panel survey of participants from the United States and South Korea, we examined both between- and within-person dynamics. Results showed that individuals with higher trait-level communication anxiety tended to use ChatGPT more frequently for communication tasks, whereas within-person fluctuations in anxiety did not predict greater use. ChatGPT use was positively associated with the satisfaction of basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence, and relatedness – and this need satisfaction, in turn, was associated with greater psychological reliance on ChatGPT. Importantly, need satisfaction further mediated the relationship between ChatGPT use and psychological reliance at both within- and between-person levels. Cultural comparisons revealed that US participants exhibited stronger momentary effects, while Korean participants showed more stable, trait-based patterns. These findings highlight the role of LLM-based chatbots as need-supportive communication tools that may become integrated into users’ communication practices over time, with implications for theories of AI-mediated communication, cross-cultural research, and the design of human-AI communication systems.

items.title: FROM DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION TO AI-ENABLED EDUCATION: A CRITICAL REVIEW OF EMERGING TRENDS, OPPORTUNITIES, AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: The higher education sector has seen the emergence of several technological advancements over the past two decades. These include learning management systems, massive open online courses, and the latest on the market: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). This paper aims to make a critical review of the shift from Digital Transformation to AI-driven education as a whole. The paper particularly emphasizes the shift of the digital transformation from being an administrative phenomenon to being more of a central feature in education. The paper summarises the literature on the concepts of digital transformation, the implementation of generative AI, and adaptive learning and AI ethics in the teaching and learning process, based on peer-reviewed papers that were mainly published in Scopus and Web of Science from 2019 to 2026. There are three themes that are repeated in the literature. First, AI in education is a further step towards digital transformation in which capacity building processes are substituted with independent decision making. Second, personalisation, accessibility and efficiency are opportunities, not equally accessible or equally taken up, nor equally realised; and these opportunities go first to the best resourced institutions.
